passage:
I'm Shreya, and last September I was the girl who swore she'd start physics revision "properly" in October. Every evening at seven, Nazia sent the same message: "One match? Just one."
The board exam was in March, which felt like a different planet. The match was right there, loud and bright, with my team waiting. One match became four. My physics notebook sat under the charger.
I told myself a few evenings couldn't change a grade in March. Looking back, what gets me is how sharp the game felt and how blurry March felt, even though March was the thing I actually cared about. In January I counted: sixty evenings, gone. After that, the controller went into Ammi's cupboard until nine.

qa.q: Where did Shreya's physics notebook sit while she played?
qa.a: The physics notebook sat under the charger.

qa.q: Why did 'just one match' feel reasonable to Shreya each evening?
qa.a: The match was loud, bright and happening now, while the March exam felt like a different planet, so one evening seemed too small to matter.

qa.q: Which choice finally helped Shreya, and why could it work?
qa.a: Putting the controller in Ammi's cupboard until nine meant she no longer had to win the fight with herself every evening; the study hour came first by default.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel if Shreya starts saying no to the seven o'clock match?
qa.a: Nazia might miss their evening game or feel a bit let down at first, but could also be pushed to think about the same exam.

grounding: Shows a teenager choosing a nightly game over revision because the exam months away feels faint compared with the fun right now.

passage:
Mentor note: Tejas, Class 10, 14 November
Tejas came to the after-school study room today, sat down with his maths sheet, and within ten minutes was watching a friend's game on his phone under the desk. When I asked, he said, "The prelims are in February, ma'am. One round now won't matter."
He isn't careless. He told me he really wants the science seat next year. But the seat feels far off, and the game is happening right now.
We agreed on one change: his phone stays in my tray for the first forty minutes, and he has written the prelim date and the seat he wants on a sticky note on his desk. If he finishes the sheet, he gets the phone back for fifteen minutes of play.
Vinita, class mentor

qa.q: What did Tejas say when Vinita asked about the phone?
qa.a: He said, "The prelims are in February, ma'am. One round now won't matter."

qa.q: Why does 'one round' seem harmless to Tejas even though he wants the science seat?
qa.a: The seat is months away and feels vague, while the game is vivid and happening now, so a single round looks too small to cost anything.

qa.q: Why might the phone tray and the sticky note help Tejas?
qa.a: The tray removes the pull of the game for forty minutes, the note keeps the goal in view, and the fifteen minutes of play give him a reward he can feel today.

qa.q: How does Vinita view Tejas, and why does that matter for him?
qa.a: Vinita sees him as someone who wants the seat, not a careless student, so Tejas gets a practical plan instead of a lecture and is more likely to try it.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who lets a game win over studying because the future result seems distant and weak.

passage:
Wed night, 11:40
Dear diary, today's score: chemistry 0, game 3 hours. 😅
The unit test that decides my term grade is two months away. Two months! My brain treats it like a rumour.
At 8 I opened the textbook. At 8:05 Shreya knocked: "New season's out, want to see my squad?" I said ten minutes.
Those ten minutes had music and fireworks and a rank-up. The chemistry chapter had moles.
Now it's late and I feel a bit sick, like I've borrowed time from some future Nazia who will have to pay it back.
Tomorrow: textbook first, one match after. Writing it here so I can't pretend I didn't.
Nazia

qa.q: What time did Nazia open the textbook?
qa.a: At 8, and at 8:05 Shreya knocked.

qa.q: How can you tell that Nazia feels uneasy about the evening?
qa.a: Nazia writes about feeling a bit sick and about borrowing time from a future Nazia who will have to pay it back.

qa.q: What is Nazia's plan for tomorrow, and why might it work better?
qa.a: Textbook first and one match after turns the game into a reward for studying, instead of something that eats the study time.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel if Nazia answers the knock tomorrow with 'textbook first'?
qa.a: Shreya might be a little let down at not showing the new squad straight away, but they could still enjoy one match together once Nazia's study time is done.

grounding: Shows a teen whose test two months away feels unreal next to a new game season happening tonight.

passage:
After school in the small town of Rahuri, the cyber café behind the bus stand was the only place with fast internet. Devika, fifteen, went there every day at four to play a racing game with the boys from Class 10.
Her friend Manjula found her there on a Wednesday in November. "The science practical file is due in March, and Sir said the board marks count for college."
"March," Devika said, eyes on the screen. "That's four months. This is the final lap."
"You said that last week."
"I'll do the whole file over Diwali."
Manjula sat on the plastic stool beside her and waited. The race ended. Devika bought another half hour with her bus money and said she'd walk home.
Manjula walked with her, carrying both their bags, the empty practical file sticking out of Devika's.

qa.q: What did Devika buy with her bus money?
qa.a: Another half hour at the cyber café.

qa.q: Why does Devika keep choosing the game over the practical file?
qa.a: The final lap is exciting and happening now, while March and college marks feel four months away and not quite real, so the game keeps winning.

qa.q: What choice could Devika make on the next Wednesday to help herself?
qa.a: She could do one page of the practical file with Manjula before going to the café, and let the game be the reward afterwards.

qa.q: What is the walk home like for Manjula?
qa.a: Manjula carries both bags and sees the empty practical file, likely feeling worried for Devika and unsure how to get through to her.

grounding: It shows a teenager preferring gaming now over better marks months later, because distant benefits feel weak and the game feels vivid.
